about: The expert council, item 6 (queue expert-council): decide once. Good investors write a decision down before they make it (what they expect, why, and what would prove them wrong), run a pre-mortem, and set a date to review it; psychologists add that the best way to avoid deciding badly when tired is to decide in advance, as a standing rule. Two parts: standing rules that settle recurring choices once, and a journal for the few big ones. Paraphrased from common practice; content only, the screen is not built yet. Not financial or legal advice.

loop.cue: A big decision appears (the test below says which), and the review date of an old one arrives in the calendar (dated items through gmCalendarDated).
loop.smallestStep: Three lines: what I am deciding, what I expect to happen, and when I will check. Two minutes.
loop.reward: At review, the app shows what you expected next to what happened; a decision reviewed counts, whatever the result.
loop.environment: The journal opens from the screens where big decisions start (a loan, a job offer, a large purchase, a property).
loop.review: Each decision on its own date; once a year, read the year's decisions in one sitting and name one pattern.
loop.constraint: Honesty at review: judge the decision by what was known then, not by the outcome alone.

isItBig.say: Use the journal when any one of these is true; otherwise decide quickly and move on.

tests.text: It is hard or costly to undo (a job, a home, a marriage of money, a move, a surgery by choice).
It is more than one month of take-home, or it adds a loan.
It commits more than a year of your time or attention.
It changes life for someone else in the family.
You feel rushed, flattered, afraid of missing out, or angry.

entry.ask: What exactly am I deciding, in one sentence?
What are at least two other options, including doing nothing?
What do I expect to happen, by when, and how sure am I (a percentage)?
How does this usually turn out for people like me? (The outside view.)
It is a year from now and this went badly. What are the three most likely reasons?
For the likeliest reason: what can I do now to prevent it, or to limit the loss?
What would make me change my mind or stop? Name the sign and the number.
How am I feeling right now: rested, tired, pressed, excited?

entry.default: 90 days for money and work; 12 months for a home or a life change

biasChecks.ask: If I were starting fresh today, would I still choose this?
Am I doing this because others are?
Whose first number am I measuring against, and is it a fair one?
What would a careful friend say I am too sure about?
Am I avoiding a small sure loss by risking a large one?
Who gains if I decide today rather than next week?

reviewQuestions: What happened, against what I expected?
Was the decision good given what I knew, whatever the result? (Good decision and good luck are different things.)
What did I not know that I could have found out cheaply?
One rule I will keep from this.

standingRules.say: Decide once, in a calm hour, and stop deciding each time. Pick the ones that fit; change any number.

rules.rule: Any unplanned purchase above {amount} waits 48 hours.
Saving and investing leave the account on salary day, automatically; spending is what remains.
No investment on a tip or a forwarded message. Anything new is read about for a week and is at most {share} of investments.
The portfolio is looked at for changes once a year, in the birthday month, not when markets move.
I do not stand guarantor or lend more than I can afford to lose, and I say so kindly, once.
No resignation, angry message or big yes on the same day: sleep on it.
Anyone who asks for money, a code or a secret by phone or message is called back on a number I already have. No exceptions for urgency or rank.
No advance, token or signature on a property or agreement before the papers are read by someone who knows them.
A check-up due this month is booked before anything optional is.
If I would not say yes to it for tomorrow, I do not say yes to it for three months from now.

persona.who: A person offered a new job abroad
A person who buys on impulse
A retired person called by a 'bank officer'
